claims.text: The x = 0.40 baseline alloy predominantly has a hexagonal Ni2In-type structure with a small amount of orthorhombic TiNiSi-type phase.
The x = 0.40 baseline exhibits a strong first-order magnetostructural transition.
The x = 0.40 baseline exhibits a large magnetocaloric response but limited mechanical integrity.
The proposed intervention is to replace Ni with Co by increasing x from 0.40 to approximately 0.50 while retaining the stated melting, annealing, and quenching protocol.
Increasing x to approximately 0.50 will slightly increase the hexagonal lattice ratio c_hex/a_hex.
Increasing x to approximately 0.50 will stabilize the high-temperature hexagonal Ni2In-type phase.
The proposed substitution will preserve lattice distortions and phase coexistence needed for a first-order magnetostructural transition.
Replacing Ni with Co enhances covalent bonding between neighboring Mn atoms.
The enhanced bonding stabilizes the Ni2In-type austenite.
The proposed Co substitution reduces internal stresses.
Reduced internal stresses and altered bonding strengthen the alloy.
At x approximately equal to 0.50, first-order magnetostructural coupling will be retained.
Retained first-order magnetostructural coupling will generate large latent heat and a giant magnetocaloric effect.
Relative to x = 0.40, the x approximately equal to 0.50 alloy will have increased hardness.
Relative to x = 0.40, the x approximately equal to 0.50 alloy will have increased compressive strength.
The x approximately equal to 0.50 alloy will preserve a large magnetocaloric response under magnetic fields up to 5 T within 183–400 K, particularly near 295–310 K.
Increasing x to 0.55 will shift the transition from first order to second order.
A second-order transition at x = 0.55 would reduce latent heat and lower the caloric response.
Processing variations or compositional inhomogeneity could alter phase coupling and transition sharpness.
